title: ר' שמלאי מלוד

paragraphs:
R' Simlai of Lod, whose residence was in Nehardea. R' Yohanan did not wish to teach him the Book of Genealogies: Pesahim 62b. Its wording is: R' Simlai came before R' Yohanan and said, “Let the master teach me the Book of Genealogies.” He asked, “Where are you from?” He answered, “From Lod.” “Where is your residence?” He answered, “In Nehardea.” He said, “We do not teach either the people of Lod or the Nehardeans”—Rashi explains that he intended to put him off, or alternatively, because their lineage is not distinguished—“and all the more so you, who are from Lod and reside in Nehardea.” He pressed and persuaded him. He said, “Teach it to me in three months.” He took a clod and threw it at him, saying, “If even Beruryah ….” He asked, “My master, what is the difference between for its own sake and not for its own sake …?” He answered, “Since you are a Torah scholar ….”

This requires examination: why did Rashi not explain the reason that one does not teach the people of Lod, and so forth, from what appears in Jerusalem Pesahim, Tamid Nishhat, halakhah 3? R' Simlai came to R' Yonatan and said, “Teach me aggadah.” He answered, “I have a tradition from my forebears not to teach aggadah either to a Babylonian or to a Southerner, for they are arrogant and deficient in Torah; you are a Nehardean and live in the South.” He said, “Tell me this matter: what is the difference between for its own sake and not for its own sake …?” One cannot say that this is a different incident because the Bavli says “Teach the Book of Genealogies,” whereas the Jerusalem Talmud says aggadah, for the Book of Genealogies too consists of aggadah.

(As for its mentioning in the Bavli that he asked R' Yonatan: such is the Jerusalem Talmud's way, to mention a different amora's name. But it is plausible that in the Bavli too it should read that he asked R' Yonatan, for nowhere in the Talmud do we find R' Simlai asking R' Yohanan. We do find in Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 49, that R' Simlai asked R' Yonatan the meaning of “There is one swept away without justice.” There is supporting evidence that he asked R' Yonatan to study aggadah with him, for R' Shmuel bar Nahman was R' Yonatan's pupil; see his entry. We find R' Helbo saying to R' Shmuel bar Nahmani [contextual proposal; digital witness רשב״ג, perhaps for רשב״נ], and likewise R' Yehudah the Nasi and R' Shimon ben Yehotzadak saying, “I have heard about you that you are a master of aggadah.” Presumably, then, he learned aggadah from his teacher R' Yonatan.) See Jerusalem Sanhedrin, first chapter, halakhah 2: Lod is in Yehudah; why do they not intercalate the year there? Because they are arrogant and deficient in Torah. Thus R' Simlai was from Lod, whose people are arrogant and deficient in Torah, and for that reason they are not taught. Therefore R' Simlai asked him the difference between “for its own sake,” and so forth; then R' Y. said, “He is a Torah scholar.” Why did Rashi write the reason that their lineage is not distinguished? This requires examination.

The reason that one does not teach aggadah to the arrogant seems to me to be what appears at the end of Ein Doreshin: “a support of water”—these are masters of aggadah. It is known that humility is learned from water, which leaves a high place and descends to a low one. Thus the arrogant are deficient in Torah, for Torah endures only in the lowliest of vessels. Perhaps it is one matter: just as the Holy One, blessed be He, does not dwell with the arrogant—“him I cannot bear”—so the Holy One, blessed be He, dwells only with those of distinguished lineage among Israel. In Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu, chapter 18, brought in Yalkut, II Samuel, chapter 20: if someone possesses proper conduct and Scripture alone, one angel is assigned to him, and so forth. If he has read Tanakh, two angels are assigned to him. But if he has read Tanakh, Mishnah, midrash, halakhot, and aggadot, the Holy One, blessed be He, guards him Himself, and so forth. Intercalation of a year must also be specifically in the Land of Israel, because the Lord's eyes are always there. Thus in a place of arrogant people one cannot intercalate years, because “him I cannot bear.” This justifies what is said in Yalkut Tehillim, chapter 28, on “For they do not understand the works of the Lord”: Hizkiyah said, “These are the seasons”; R' Yehoshua ben Levi said, “These are the aggadot,” and so forth. One master said one thing and the other another, and they do not disagree: where aggadah may not be learned because of arrogance, there years are not intercalated on account of the season. וק״ל [provisionally: this is readily understood]. This is the intention of Sifrei, Ekev, on “everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord”: these are halakhot and aggadot. Do you wish to know Him who created the world? Learn aggadah; see there. I have gone beyond my bounds to show that R' Y. did not merely put R' Simlai off; rather, it is actually so: Lod's people are arrogant, and one does not teach aggadah to the arrogant. This R' Simlai is the one mentioned previously; Yuhasin erred, as above.
